entity_document.title: DaVita
entity_document.text:
<<QA_RELEVANT>>DaVita Inc. (a shortened contraction of "dare vita, meaning "to give life" in the Italian language), incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Denver, provides kidney dialysis services through a network of 2,657 outpatient centers in the United States, serving 200,500 patients (36% of the total of 557,000 patients in the U.S.), and 585 outpatient centers in 14 other countries serving 94,500 patients.[2] The company primarily treats end-stage renal disease (ESRD), which requires patients to undergo kidney dialysis, often 3 times per week for the rest of their lives unless they receive a kidney transplant via organ donation.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>On February 27, 1998, the company acquired Renal Treatment Centers for $1.3 billion in stock.[4][7] The integration went poorly and in July 1999, the CEO and CFO resigned.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After tripling in value between 1995 and 1998, by July 1999, the stock price was down 71% year-to-date.[8][9] In October 1999, Kent J.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Thiry, then 43 years old, was named CEO.[10]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2014, DaVita acquired Colorado Springs Health Partners, with 600 employees and 110,000 patients.[16]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2012, DaVita acquired Healthcare Partners for $4.42 billion, which was renamed DaVita Medical Group.[14] In June 2019, the division was sold to UnitedHealth Group for $4.3 billion.[15]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In July 2021, a federal grand jury indicted DaVita and former CEO Kent Thiry on charges of labor market collusion alleging participation in conspiracies with Surgical Care Affiliates to suppress competition for the services of certain senior-level employees.[23] The company and Thiry were acquitted by a jury in April 2022.[24][25] In October 2021, the Federal Trade Commission imposed limits on the company engaging in more mergers in Utah because of its history of buying up competitors.[26]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2025, 68% of the company's revenues came from Medicare and other government-based health insurance programs.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2025, 89% of the company's patients were covered by government-based health insurance programs.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Commercial payers, which accounted for 32% of revenues in 2025, generate nearly all of the company's profit as they reimburse at a much higher rate than government-based health insurance programs.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>In 2000, the company sold its non-U.S. operations.[11] In October 2000, the company was renamed DaVita Inc.[12]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In June 2018, a jury awarded the families of 3 of the company's patients $383 million in wrongful death claims after the patients died from cardiac arrest after undergoing treatment at DaVita centers.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2024, the Federal Trade Commission began investigating Davita along with Fresenius Medical Care under allegations they use illegal tactics to push smaller companies out of the market.[27]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In May 2025, the benefits fund of the United Food and Commercial Workers Local 1776 filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against DaVita and Fresenius Medical Care, a rival dialysis provider, alleging that the two companies illegally conspired to inflate treatment costs.[28]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In August 1994, 70% of the company was acquired by DLJ Merchant Banking Partners in a leveraged buyout for $75.5 million,[5] including a $10.5 million investment by DLJ.[6] The company then changed its name to Total Renal Care Holdings, Inc.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In March 2016, it acquired the Everett Clinic Medical Group, a 20-site physicians practice with 315,000 patients in the Seattle area, for $385 million.[17]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In June 2015, the company agreed to pay $450 million to settle allegations that it unnecessarily disposed of drugs and then billed the U.S. federal government for this waste.[20]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In October 2018, it agreed to pay $270 million to settle allegations that it violated the False Claims Act by providing inaccurate information that caused Medicare Advantage Plans to receive inflated payments.<</Q_RELEVANT>> James Swoben, a whistleblower, received $10 million.[22]

property_documents.title: Denver County
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver's west-central geographic location in the Mountain Time Zone (UTC−7) also benefits the telecommunications industry by allowing communication with both North American coasts, South America, Europe, and Asia on the same business day.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver's location on the 105th meridian at over one mile (1.6 km) in elevation also enables it to be the largest city in the U.S. to offer a "one-bounce" real-time satellite uplink to six continents in the same business day.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Qwest Communications now part of CenturyLink, Dish Network Corporation, Starz, DIRECTV, and Comcast are a few of the many telecommunications companies with operations in the Denver area.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>These and other high-tech companies had a boom in Denver in the mid to late 1990s.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After a rise in unemployment in the Great Recession, Denver's unemployment rate recovered and had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the nation at 2.6% in November 2016.[122] As of December 2016, the unemployment rate for the Denver–Aurora–Broomfield MSA is 2.6%.[123] The Downtown region has seen increased real estate investment[124][needs update] with the construction of several new skyscrapers from 2010 onward and major development around Denver Union Station.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

On November 22, 1858,[contradictory] General William Larimer and Captain Jonathan Cox, both land speculators from eastern Kansas Territory, placed cottonwood logs to stake a claim on the bluff overlooking the confluence of the South Platte River and Cherry Creek, across the creek from the existing mining settlement of Auraria, and on the site of the existing townsite of St. Charles. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Larimer named the townsite Denver City to curry favor with Kansas Territorial Governor James W.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver.[31] Larimer hoped the town's name would help it be selected as the county seat of Arapahoe County, but unbeknownst to him, Governor Denver had already resigned from office.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The location was accessible to existing trails and was across the South Platte River from the site of seasonal encampments of the Cheyenne and Arapaho.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The site of these first towns is now occupied by Confluence Park near downtown Denver.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Edward W. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Wynkoop came to Colorado in 1859 and became one of the city's founders.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Wynkoop Street in Denver is named after him.[32][33]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver is home to a wide array of museums.[135] Many are nationally recognized, including a new wing for the Denver Art Museum by architect Daniel Libeskind, the nation's second-largest Performing Arts Center after Lincoln Center in New York City, and bustling neighborhoods such as LoDo, filled with art galleries, restaurants, bars and clubs.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>That is part of the reason Denver was, in 2006, recognized for the third year in a row as the best city for singles.[136] Its neighborhoods also continue their influx of diverse people and businesses while the city's cultural institutions grow and prosper.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The city acquired the estate of abstract expressionist painter Clyfford Still in 2004 and built a museum to exhibit his works near the Denver Art Museum.[137] The Denver Museum of Nature and Science holds an aquamarine specimen valued at over $1 million, as well as specimens of the state mineral, rhodochrosite.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Every September the Denver Mart, at 451 E. 58th Avenue, hosts a gem and mineral show.[138] The state history museum, History Colorado Center, opened in April 2012.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It features hands-on and interactive exhibits, artifacts and programs about Colorado history.[139] It was named in 2013 by True West Magazine as one of the top-ten "must see" history museums in the country.[140] History Colorado's Byers-Evans House Museum and the Molly Brown House are nearby.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Over the years, the city has been home to other large corporations in the central United States, making Denver a key trade point for the country.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Several well-known companies originated in or have relocated to Denver.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>William Ainsworth opened the Denver Instrument Company in 1895 to make analytical balances for gold assayers.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Its factory is now in Arvada. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Aimco is headquartered in Denver.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Samsonite began in Denver in 1910 as Shwayder Trunk Manufacturing Company, but Samsonite closed its NE Denver factory in 2001, and moved its headquarters to Massachusetts after a change of ownership in 2006.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Qwest Corporation, founded in Denver in 1911 as Mountain States Telephone & Telegraph Company, is now a part of Lumen Technologies (previously CenturyLink).<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver has also enjoyed success as a pioneer in the fast-casual restaurant industry, with many popular national chain restaurants founded and based in Denver.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Quiznos and Smashburger were founded and headquartered in Denver.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>Qdoba Mexican Grill, Noodles & Company, and Good Times Burgers & Frozen Custard originated in Denver, but have moved their headquarters to the suburbs of Wheat Ridge, Broomfield, and Golden, respectively.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Chipotle Mexican Grill was founded in Denver, but moved its headquarters to Newport Beach, California in 2018.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE, nicknamed "the Big Board")[4] is an American stock exchange headquartered at the New York Stock Exchange Building in the Financial District of Lower Manhattan in New York City.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is the largest stock exchange in the world by market capitalization,[5][6][7] exceeding $44 trillion in January 2026.[8] The NYSE is owned by Intercontinental Exchange, an American holding company that it also lists (ticker symbol ICE).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Previously, it was part of NYSE Euronext (NYX), which was formed by the NYSE's 2007 merger with Euronext.[9] According to a Gallup poll conducted in 2022, approximately 58% of American adults reported having money invested in the stock market, either through individual stocks, mutual funds, or retirement accounts.[10]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>In the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, the NYSE was closed for four trading sessions, resuming on Monday, September 17, one of the rare times the NYSE was closed for more than one session and only the third time since March 1933.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>On the first day, the NYSE suffered a 7.1% drop in value (684 points); after a week, it dropped by 14% (1,370 points).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>An estimated $1.4 trillion was lost within five days of trading.[29] The NYSE was only 5 blocks from Ground Zero.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The same day it was announced that the exchange and the New York Stock Exchange building would be closed to the general public, a practice that continues to the present day.[30]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Many of the people who ring the bell are business executives whose companies trade on the exchange, usually to announce new products, acquisitions, mergers or public offerings.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, there have also been many famous people from outside the world of business that have rung the bell, such as the Mayor of New York City Rudy Giuliani and the President of South Africa Nelson Mandela.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Two United Nations Secretaries General have also rung the bell. <<Q_RELEVANT>>On April 27, 2006, Secretary-General Kofi Annan rang the opening bell to launch the United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment.[85] On July 24, 2013, Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon rang the closing bell to celebrate the NYSE joining the United Nations Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative.[86] President-Elect Donald Trump rang the bell on December 12, 2024, after being named the Time Person of the Year.[87]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The main New York Stock Exchange Building, built in 1903, is at 18 Broad Street, between the corners of Wall Street and Exchange Place, and was designed in the Beaux Arts style by George B.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Post.[40] The adjacent structure at 11 Wall Street, completed in 1922, was designed in a similar style by Trowbridge & Livingston.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The buildings were both designated a National Historic Landmark in 1978.[41][42][43] 18 Broad Street is also a New York City designated landmark.[44]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The earliest recorded organization of securities trading in New York among brokers directly dealing with each other can be traced to the Buttonwood Agreement.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Previously, securities exchange had been intermediated by auctioneers, who also conducted more mundane auctions of commodities such as wheat and tobacco.[11] On May 17, 1792, twenty-four brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement, which set a floor commission rate charged to clients and bound the signers to give preference to the other signers in securities sales.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The earliest securities traded were mostly governmental securities such as War Bonds from the Revolutionary War and First Bank of the United States stock,[11] although Bank of New York stock was a non-governmental security traded in the early days.[12] The Bank of North America, along with the First Bank of the United States and the Bank of New York, were the first shares traded on the New York Stock Exchange.[13]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>The New York Stock Exchange (sometimes referred to as "The Big Board")[46] provides a means for buyers and sellers to trade shares of stock in companies registered for public trading.<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The NYSE is open for trading Monday through Friday from 9:30 am – 4:00 pm ET, with the exception of holidays declared by the Exchange in advance.[a] Proposals for round-the-clock trading have been considered by NYSE.[48]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In April 2011, Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), an American futures exchange, and NASDAQ OMX Group had together made an unsolicited proposal to buy NYSE Euronext for approximately $11 billion, a deal in which NASDAQ would have taken control of the stock exchanges.[81] NYSE Euronext rejected this offer twice, and it was finally terminated after the United States Department of Justice indicated their intention to block the deal due to antitrust concerns.[81]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver's west-central geographic location in the Mountain Time Zone (UTC−7) also benefits the telecommunications industry by allowing communication with both North American coasts, South America, Europe, and Asia on the same business day.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver's location on the 105th meridian at over one mile (1.6 km) in elevation also enables it to be the largest city in the U.S. to offer a "one-bounce" real-time satellite uplink to six continents in the same business day.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Qwest Communications now part of CenturyLink, Dish Network Corporation, Starz, DIRECTV, and Comcast are a few of the many telecommunications companies with operations in the Denver area.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>These and other high-tech companies had a boom in Denver in the mid to late 1990s.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After a rise in unemployment in the Great Recession, Denver's unemployment rate recovered and had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the nation at 2.6% in November 2016.[122] As of December 2016, the unemployment rate for the Denver–Aurora–Broomfield MSA is 2.6%.[123] The Downtown region has seen increased real estate investment[124][needs update] with the construction of several new skyscrapers from 2010 onward and major development around Denver Union Station.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

On November 22, 1858,[contradictory] General William Larimer and Captain Jonathan Cox, both land speculators from eastern Kansas Territory, placed cottonwood logs to stake a claim on the bluff overlooking the confluence of the South Platte River and Cherry Creek, across the creek from the existing mining settlement of Auraria, and on the site of the existing townsite of St. Charles. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Larimer named the townsite Denver City to curry favor with Kansas Territorial Governor James W.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver.[31] Larimer hoped the town's name would help it be selected as the county seat of Arapahoe County, but unbeknownst to him, Governor Denver had already resigned from office.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The location was accessible to existing trails and was across the South Platte River from the site of seasonal encampments of the Cheyenne and Arapaho.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The site of these first towns is now occupied by Confluence Park near downtown Denver.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Edward W. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Wynkoop came to Colorado in 1859 and became one of the city's founders.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Wynkoop Street in Denver is named after him.[32][33]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver is home to a wide array of museums.[135] Many are nationally recognized, including a new wing for the Denver Art Museum by architect Daniel Libeskind, the nation's second-largest Performing Arts Center after Lincoln Center in New York City, and bustling neighborhoods such as LoDo, filled with art galleries, restaurants, bars and clubs.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>That is part of the reason Denver was, in 2006, recognized for the third year in a row as the best city for singles.[136] Its neighborhoods also continue their influx of diverse people and businesses while the city's cultural institutions grow and prosper.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The city acquired the estate of abstract expressionist painter Clyfford Still in 2004 and built a museum to exhibit his works near the Denver Art Museum.[137] The Denver Museum of Nature and Science holds an aquamarine specimen valued at over $1 million, as well as specimens of the state mineral, rhodochrosite.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Every September the Denver Mart, at 451 E. 58th Avenue, hosts a gem and mineral show.[138] The state history museum, History Colorado Center, opened in April 2012.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It features hands-on and interactive exhibits, artifacts and programs about Colorado history.[139] It was named in 2013 by True West Magazine as one of the top-ten "must see" history museums in the country.[140] History Colorado's Byers-Evans House Museum and the Molly Brown House are nearby.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In most Western orthographies, the ſ gradually fell out of use during the second half of the 18th century, although it remained in occasional use into the 19th century.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In Spain, the change was mainly accomplished between 1760 and 1766.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In France, the change occurred between 1782 and 1793. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Printers in the United States stopped using the long s between 1795 and 1810.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In English orthography, the London printer John Bell (1745–1831) pioneered the change. <<QA_RELEVANT>>His edition of Shakespeare, in 1785, was advertised with the claim that he "ventured to depart from the common mode by rejecting the long 'ſ' in favor of the round one, as being less liable to error....."[5] The Times of London made the switch from the long to the short s with its issue of 10 September 1803.<</QA_RELEVANT>> Encyclopædia Britannica's 5th edition, completed in 1817, was the last edition to use the long s.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In Portuguese, it may represent the voiceless palato-alveolar fricative /ʃ/ in most dialects when syllable-final, and [ʒ] in European Portuguese Islão (Islam) or, in many sociolects of Brazilian Portuguese, esdrúxulo (proparoxytone).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, when the next word starts with a vowel, this /ʃ/ is turned into [z] in all dialects.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>The former stadium of FC Porto, Estádio das Antas, was sometimes mispronounced with three instances of [ʃ] by foreign commentators, while the native pronunciation is [ɨʃˈtaðju ðɐz ˈɐ̃tɐʃ] (where a phonetic [ʃ] appears before a consonant and a pause, respectively).<</QA_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In Brazilian dialects without the retraction, ⟨s⟩ in das is pronounced the same in this phrase, [isˈtadʒiu daz ˈɐ̃tɐs], with differences lying elsewhere.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The minuscule form  ſ, called the long s, developed in the early medieval period, within the Visigothic and Carolingian hands, with predecessors in the half-uncial and cursive scripts of Late Antiquity.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It remained standard in western writing throughout the medieval period and was adopted in early printing with movable types.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It existed alongside minuscule "round" or "short" s, which were at the time only used at the end of words.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>archaic Greek Sigma could be written with different numbers of angles and strokes.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Besides the classical form with four strokes (), a three-stroke form resembling an angular Latin S () was commonly found, and was particularly characteristic of some mainland Greek varieties, including the Attic and several "red" alphabets.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>archaic Greek Sigma could be written with different numbers of angles and strokes.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Besides the classical form with four strokes (), a three-stroke form resembling an angular Latin S () was commonly found, and was particularly characteristic of some mainland Greek varieties, including the Attic and several "red" alphabets.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Ancient Greek did not have a  /ʃ/ "sh" phoneme, so the derived Greek letter Sigma (Σ) came to represent the voiceless alveolar sibilant /s/.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>While the letter shape Σ continues Phoenician šîn, its name sigma is taken from the letter Samekh, while the shape and position of samekh but name of šîn is continued in the xi.[citation needed] Within Greek, the name of sigma was influenced by its association with the Greek word σίζω (earlier *sigj-), "to hiss".<</Q_RELEVANT>> The original name of the letter "Sigma" may have been san, but due to the early history of the Greek epichoric alphabets, "san" came to be identified as a separate letter, Ϻ.[3] Herodotus reported that "san" was the name given by the Dorians to the same letter called "Sigma" by the Ionians.[4]

The Western Greek alphabet used in Cumae was adopted by the Etruscans and Latins in the 7th century BC, and over the following centuries, it developed into a range of Old Italic alphabets, including the Etruscan alphabet and the early Latin alphabet. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In Etruscan, the value /s/ of Greek sigma (𐌔) was maintained, while san (𐌑) represented a separate phoneme, most likely /ʃ/ "sh" (transliterated as ś).<</Q_RELEVANT>> The early Latin alphabet adopted sigma, but not san, as Old Latin did not have a /ʃ/ "sh" phoneme.

The shape of Latin S arises from Greek Σ by dropping one out of the four strokes of that letter. The (angular) S-shape composed of three strokes existed as a variant of the four-stroke letter Σ already in the epigraphy of Western Greek alphabets, and the three and four strokes variants existed alongside one another in the classical Etruscan alphabet. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In other Italic alphabets (Venetic, Lepontic), the letter could be represented as a zig-zagging line of any number between three and six strokes.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Italic letter was also adopted into Elder Futhark, as Sowilō (ᛊ), and appears with four to eight strokes in the earliest runic inscriptions, but is occasionally reduced to three strokes (ᛋ) from the later 5th century, and appears regularly with three strokes in Younger Futhark.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Northwest Semitic šîn represented a voiceless postalveolar fricative /ʃ/ (as in 'ship').<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It originated most likely as a pictogram of a tooth (שנא) and represented the phoneme /ʃ/ via the acrophonic principle.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Most of Mexico, and most of Arizona in the United States, do not observe daylight saving time (DST), and during the spring, summer, and autumn months they are on the same time as Pacific Daylight Time.[1] The Navajo Nation is the only part of Arizona that observes DST.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its territory lies mostly within Arizona but extends into Utah and New Mexico (both observe DST statewide).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Meanwhile, the Hopi Reservation, despite being completely surrounded by the Navajo Nation, does not observe DST, and neither do some Arizona state offices located within the Navajo Nation.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Alphabetical list of major cities located within the Mountain Time Zone.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Cities in bold do not observe daylight saving time:<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>On September 24, 2020, Yukon switched to the Mountain Standard Time year-round.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Therefore, clocks in Yukon and Alberta are the same in the winter, and Alberta is one hour ahead in summer.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Previously, the territory had used the Pacific Time Zone with daylight saving time: UTC−8 in winter and UTC−7 in summer.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The clock time in this zone is based on the mean solar time at the 105th meridian west of the Greenwich Observatory.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the United States, the exact specification for the location of time zones and the dividing lines between zones is set forth in the Code of Federal Regulations at 49 CFR 71.[a]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Three states are split between the Mountain Time Zone and the Pacific Time Zone.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The following locations observe Mountain Time:<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Five states are split between the Mountain Time Zone and the Central Time Zone.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The following locations observe Mountain Time:<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Revillagigedo Islands (Colima): three of the four islands have the same time as Mountain Time Zone: Socorro Island, San Benedicto Island and Roca Partida.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>On March 8, 2026, most of British Columbia in the Pacific Time Zone adopted UTC−7 year-round but continue to call their time zone "Pacific Time".<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Southeastern parts of the province (near the Alberta border) continue to observe daylight saving time: UTC−6 in the summer and UTC−7 in the winter.[6]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The communities of Jackpot, Jarbidge, Mountain City, and Owyhee unofficially observe Mountain Time, although they are officially within the Pacific Time Zone.[7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The communities of Jackpot, Jarbidge, Mountain City, and Owyhee unofficially observe Mountain Time, although they are officially within the Pacific Time Zone.[7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In Canada, Mexico, and the United States, this time zone is generically called Mountain Time (MT).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Specifically, it is Mountain Standard Time (MST) when observing standard time, and Mountain Daylight Time (MDT) when observing daylight saving time.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The term refers to the Rocky Mountains, which range from British Columbia to New Mexico. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In Mexico, this time zone is known as the tiempo de la montaña or zona Pacífico ('Pacific Zone').<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the United States, the Mountain Time Zone is to the east of the Pacific Time Zone; in it and Canada, it is to the west of the Central Time Zone.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Mountain Time Zone of North America keeps time by subtracting seven hours from Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) when standard time (UTC−07:00) is in effect, and by subtracting six hours during daylight saving time (UTC−06:00).<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The largest city in the Mountain Time Zone is Phoenix, Arizona; the Phoenix metropolitan area is the largest metropolitan area in the zone.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The largest city that observes daylight saving time is Juárez, Chihuahua, Mexico.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>As of October 30, 2022, Mexico abandoned daylight saving time, with certain exceptions.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>James William Denver (October 23, 1817 – August 9, 1892) was an American politician, soldier, and lawyer.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>He served in the California state government, as an officer in the United States Army in two wars, and as a Democratic member of the United States House of Representatives from California.<</Q_RELEVANT>> He served as secretary and Governor of the Kansas Territory during the struggle over whether or not Kansas would be open to slavery. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The city of Denver, Colorado, is named after him.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>A few months after the start of the American Civil War in early 1861, President Abraham Lincoln commissioned Denver a brigadier general in the volunteer army on August 14.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In November 1861, he was ordered to report to Fort Scott in Kansas and in December, he assumed command of all Federal troops in Kansas. During March and April 1862 he commanded the District of Kansas until he was transferred to the District of West Tennessee. <<Q_RELEVANT>>On May 16, 1862, Denver assumed command of the 3rd Brigade/5th Division under Maj.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Gen. William T. Sherman in the midst of the Siege of Corinth. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The very next day Denver's brigade participated in the fight for Russell's House.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Though his brigade suffered no casualties in this engagement it was nonetheless one of the two brigades leading the attack.[2]  On May 27 General Sherman again selected Denver's brigade to be one of the leading units in an attack against the Double Log House.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver and Morgan L.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Smith's brigade successfully stormed the log cabin turned block house. During this engagement Major General Ulysses S. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Grant was present on the battlefield and indicated his approval of the handsome manner in which the troops behaved.[3]  After the fall of Corinth, Denver continued in command of his brigade, serving on garrison duty in Mississippi.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>During the early stages of the Vicksburg Campaign Denver was in command of the 1st Division, XVI Corps, until his resignation from the Union Army on March 5, 1863.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

In 1847, during the Mexican–American War, he recruited a company for the 12th U.S. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Volunteer Infantry and was commissioned a captain, serving under General Winfield Scott.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After the war in 1850, Denver traveled to California, where he became a trader.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver killed newspaper editor Edward Gilbert in a duel on August 2, 1852.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Later that same year, he was elected to the California State Senate.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>He was later appointed as Secretary of State of California.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 1854 he was elected to the United States Congress as a representative from California, serving from March 4, 1855 – March 3, 1857.<</Q_RELEVANT>> He was not a candidate for renomination in 1856. On April 17, 1857, President James Buchanan appointed him as Commissioner of Indian Affairs.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In November 1858, while Denver was still serving as territorial governor, William Larimer, Jr., a land speculator from Leavenworth, planted the townsite of "Denver City" along the South Platte River in Arapaho County in western Kansas Territory (the present-day state of Colorado).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Larimer chose the name "Denver" to honor the current territorial governor with the intention that the city would be chosen as the county seat of Arapaho County.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver reportedly visited Denver, Colorado, in 1875 and 1882, but complained that his visits received little affection from the residents of the city named after him.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

James W. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Denver was born near Winchester, Virginia.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>His father was born in Ireland, while his mother was of English descent.[1] He attended public schools and moved to Ohio with his parents in 1830, settling near Wilmington.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In 1841 he taught school in Missouri, and in 1844 he graduated from the Cincinnati Law School. He was admitted to the bar and practiced law near Xenia, Ohio. He moved to Platte City, Missouri, in 1845, where he continued his law practice and acting career.

(a shortened contraction of "dare vita, meaning "to give life" in the Italian language), incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Denver, provides kidney dialysis services through a network of 2,657 outpatient centers in the United States, serving 200,500 patients (36% of the total of 557,000 patients in the U.S.), and 585 outpatient centers in 14 other countries serving 94,500 patients.[2] The company primarily treats end-stage renal disease (ESRD), which requires patients to undergo kidney dialysis, often 3 times per week for the rest of their lives unless they receive a kidney transplant via organ donation.<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>On February 27, 1998, the company acquired Renal Treatment Centers for $1.3 billion in stock.[4][7] The integration went poorly and in July 1999, the CEO and CFO resigned.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After tripling in value between 1995 and 1998, by July 1999, the stock price was down 71% year-to-date.[8][9] In October 1999, Kent J.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Thiry, then 43 years old, was named CEO.[10]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2014, DaVita acquired Colorado Springs Health Partners, with 600 employees and 110,000 patients.[16]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2012, DaVita acquired Healthcare Partners for $4.42 billion, which was renamed DaVita Medical Group.[14] In June 2019, the division was sold to UnitedHealth Group for $4.3 billion.[15]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In July 2021, a federal grand jury indicted DaVita and former CEO Kent Thiry on charges of labor market collusion alleging participation in conspiracies with Surgical Care Affiliates to suppress competition for the services of certain senior-level employees.[23] The company and Thiry were acquitted by a jury in April 2022.[24][25] In October 2021, the Federal Trade Commission imposed limits on the company engaging in more mergers in Utah because of its history of buying up competitors.[26]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2025, 68% of the company's revenues came from Medicare and other government-based health insurance programs.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2025, 89% of the company's patients were covered by government-based health insurance programs.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Commercial payers, which accounted for 32% of revenues in 2025, generate nearly all of the company's profit as they reimburse at a much higher rate than government-based health insurance programs.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<QA_RELEVANT>>In 2000, the company sold its non-U.S. operations.[11] In October 2000, the company was renamed DaVita Inc.[12]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In June 2018, a jury awarded the families of 3 of the company's patients $383 million in wrongful death claims after the patients died from cardiac arrest after undergoing treatment at DaVita centers.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2024, the Federal Trade Commission began investigating Davita along with Fresenius Medical Care under allegations they use illegal tactics to push smaller companies out of the market.[27]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In May 2025, the benefits fund of the United Food and Commercial Workers Local 1776 filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against DaVita and Fresenius Medical Care, a rival dialysis provider, alleging that the two companies illegally conspired to inflate treatment costs.[28]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In August 1994, 70% of the company was acquired by DLJ Merchant Banking Partners in a leveraged buyout for $75.5 million,[5] including a $10.5 million investment by DLJ.[6] The company then changed its name to Total Renal Care Holdings, Inc.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In March 2016, it acquired the Everett Clinic Medical Group, a 20-site physicians practice with 315,000 patients in the Seattle area, for $385 million.[17]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In June 2015, the company agreed to pay $450 million to settle allegations that it unnecessarily disposed of drugs and then billed the U.S. federal government for this waste.[20]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In October 2018, it agreed to pay $270 million to settle allegations that it violated the False Claims Act by providing inaccurate information that caused Medicare Advantage Plans to receive inflated payments.<</Q_RELEVANT>> James Swoben, a whistleblower, received $10 million.[22]

question: The firm is a Delaware‑incorporated company whose Da Vinci Surgical System is named after Leonardo da Vinci, trades on a Nasdaq exchange operated by Nasdaq, Inc., and is a component of both the S&P 500 and the S&P 100. Based on its FY 2023 filing, what was its inventory turnover ratio (cost of goods sold divided by average inventory) for the fiscal year ended 2023?

entity_document.title: Intuitive Surgical
entity_document.text:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The company refined the SRI System into a prototype known originally as "Lenny" (after Leonardo da Vinci), which was ready for testing in 1997.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>As the company's prototypes became more advanced, they were named using da Vinci themes.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>One was named "Leonardo", and another was "Mona".<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The final version of the prototype was nicknamed the da Vinci Surgical System, and the name stuck when the system was eventually commercialized.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>After further testing, Intuitive Surgical began marketing this system in Europe in 1999, while awaiting FDA approval in the United States.[citation needed][7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

In 1994, Dr. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Frederic Moll became interested in the SRI System, as the device was known at the time.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>At the time, Moll was employed by Guidant.<</Q_RELEVANT>> He tried to interest Guidant in backing it but to no avail. In 1995 Moll was introduced to John Freund who had recently left Acuson Corporation. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Freund negotiated an option to acquire SRI's intellectual property and incorporated a new company that he named Intuitive Surgical Devices, Inc.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Shortly before going public, Intuitive Surgical was sued for patent infringement by Computer Motion, Inc, its chief rival.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Computer Motion had actually gotten into the robotic surgery field earlier than Intuitive Surgical, with its own system, the ZEUS Robotic Surgical System.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Although the ZEUS system was approved in Europe, the U.S. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Food and Drug Administration had not yet approved it for any procedure at the time that the FDA first approved the da Vinci system.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The uncertainty created by the litigation between the companies was a drag on each company's growth. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2003, Intuitive Surgical and Computer Motion agreed to merge, thus ending the litigation between them.[9]  The ZEUS system was ultimately phased out in favor of the da Vinci system.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Computer Motion was led by Chairman Robert Duggan from 1990 until 2003, when the two companies merged.[10]

A da Vinci Surgical System costs approximately $1.5 million.[17] The da Vinci SI released in April 2009 cost about $1.75 million. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In addition, there are maintenance contracts plus expenditures for instruments used during surgery.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<QA_RELEVANT>>In 2008, The New York Times reported that most hospitals and clinics have a hard time recovering the cost of the robot.[16]<</QA_RELEVANT>>

Before the buyout of Computer Motion, the stock of Intuitive was selling at around $14 per share, adjusted for stock splits. <<Q_RELEVANT>>After the merger, the stock price rose significantly (and by 2015 it was at about $500),[11] primarily because of the growth in systems sold (60 in 2002 compared with 431 in 2014) and the number of surgical procedures performed (less than 1,000 in 2002 compared with 540,000 in 2014).[citation needed]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

In 2021, Intuitive was sued for alleged abuse of its monopolist position. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Specifically, replacement part manufacturer Rebotix Repair accused Intuitive of anticompetitive behavior in the robots' aftermarket business and overcharging of hospitals for replacement parts.[citation needed] The initiative was followed up by a wave of similar class-action lawsuits shortly afterwards, including those filed by Kaleida Health and Franciscan Health.[21][22] In August of 2022, Rebotix v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Intuitive settled out of court shortly before trial was set to begin.[23][24]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Intuitive Surgical, Inc. is an American biotechnology company that develops, manufactures, and markets robotic products designed to improve clinical outcomes of patients through minimally invasive surgery, most notably with the da Vinci Surgical System.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The company is part of the Nasdaq-100, S&P 100 and S&P 500. <<Q_RELEVANT>>As of 31 December 2021[update], Intuitive Surgical had an installed base of 6,730 da Vinci Surgical Systems, including 4,139 in the U.S., 1,199 in Europe, 1,050 in Asia, and 342 in the rest of the world.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Intuitive Surgical first appeared on the Fortune 500 in 2024 at number 497; in 2025 the company rose to number 459 overall and ranked 43rd within the healthcare sector.[3][4]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>For the fiscal year 2017, Intuitive Surgical reported earnings of US$660 million, with an annual revenue of US$3.129 billion, an increase of 15.7% over the previous fiscal cycle.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Intuitive Surgical's shares traded at over $307 per share, and its market capitalization was valued at over US$58 billion in November 2018.[12]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In June 2018, Intuitive Surgical settled class action suits of its shareholders for a payment of $43 million.[18][19] Originally filed in 2013, shareholders alleged Intuitive Surgical failed to report injuries related to their da Vinci robot, thus violating federal security laws. [20]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Sultzer v. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Intuitive Surgical, Inc. involved a claim against Intuitive that a defect in its da Vinci surgical robot allowed electricity to arc through a patient's spine, resulting in her death.[25] Intuitive was represented by Bradley Arant Boult Cummings.[25] On July 12, 2024, the plaintiff agreed to drop the case.[25]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Significantly, Delaware has one of the few remaining Courts of Chancery in the nation, which has jurisdiction over equity cases, the vast majority of which are corporate disputes, many relating to mergers and acquisitions.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Court of Chancery and the Delaware Supreme Court have developed a worldwide reputation for rendering concise opinions concerning corporate law which generally (but not always) grant broad discretion to corporate boards of directors and officers.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In addition, the Delaware General Corporation Law, which forms the basis of the Courts' opinions, is widely regarded as giving great flexibility to corporations to manage their affairs.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>For these reasons, Delaware is considered to have the most business-friendly legal system in the United States; therefore a great number of companies are incorporated in Delaware, including 60% of the companies listed on the New York Stock Exchange.[175]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware (/ˈdɛləwɛər/ ⓘ DEL-ə-wair)[10] is a state in the Mid-Atlantic and South Atlantic[11] regions of the United States.[12] It borders Maryland to its south and west, Pennsylvania to its north, New Jersey to its northeast, and the Atlantic Ocean to its east.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The state's name derives from the adjacent Delaware Bay, which in turn was named after Thomas West, 3rd Baron De La Warr, an English nobleman and the Colony of Virginia's first colonial-era governor.[13]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware was named after its location on the Delaware Bay, which in turn derived its name from Thomas West, 3rd Baron De La Warr (1577–1618), the first governor of the Colony of Virginia.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Delaware people, a name used by Europeans for Lenape people Indigenous to the Delaware Valley, also derive their name from the same source.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Like in World War I, the state enjoyed a big stimulus to its gunpowder and shipyard industries in World War II. <<Q_RELEVANT>>New job opportunities during and after the war in the Wilmington area coaxed Black people from the southern counties to move to the city.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The proportion of blacks constituting the city's population rose from 15% in 1950 to over 50% by 1980.[48] The surge of Black migrants to the north sparked white flight, in which middle class whites moved from the city to suburban areas, leading to de facto segregation of Northern Delaware's society.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the 1940s and 1950s, Delaware attempted to integrate its schools, although the last segregated school in the state did not close until 1970.[49] The University of Delaware admitted its first black student in 1948, and local courts ruled that primary schools had to be integrated.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware's integration efforts partially inspired the US Supreme Court's decision in Brown v.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Board of Education, which found racial segregation in United States public schools to be unconstitutional.[50] The result of the Brown ruling was that Delaware became fully integrated, albeit with time and much effort.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware's population mainly consisted of people from the British Isles, African slaves, Germans and a few remaining Native Americans during the colonial era.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Irish, Germans, Italians, Poles, and Russian Jewish immigrants were attracted by the industries in the Wilmington area. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the late 20th century a Puerto Rican community formed in Wilmington.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Guatemalan people migrated to Sussex county to work in Delaware's poultry industry.<</Q_RELEVANT>> There is also a small numbers of Asians in New Castle county who work as scientific and engineering professionals.[92]

However, by 1704 the province of Pennsylvania had grown so large their representatives wanted to make decisions without the assent of the Lower Counties, and the two groups of representatives began meeting on their own, one at Philadelphia, and the other at New Castle. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Penn and his heirs remained proprietors of both and always appointed the same person Governor for their province of Pennsylvania and their territory of the Lower Counties.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The fact that Delaware and Pennsylvania shared the same governor was not unique; from 1703 to 1738, New York and New Jersey shared a governor.[26] Massachusetts and New Hampshire also shared a governor for some time.[27]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2019, WEX opened a new 100,000-square-foot headquarters across from the Ocean Gateway International Marine Passenger Terminal in Portland, Maine.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The company continues to have a significant presence in South Portland.[9] WEX is one of 10 founding corporate partners of the Roux Institute at Northeastern University, which leases a portion of the WEX headquarters for its campus.[10]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In October 1954, the city of Milford became the scene of one of the country's first pro-segregation boycotts after eleven Black students were enrolled in the previously all-white Milford High School.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Mass protests continued in Milford; the school board eventually ceded to the protestors, expelling the Black students.[51][52][53] The ensuing unrest, which included cross burnings, rallies, and pro-segregation demonstrations, contributed to desegregation in most of Southern Delaware being delayed for another ten years.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Sussex County did not start closing or integrating its segregated schools until 1965, 11 years after the Brown ruling.[54] Throughout the state, integration only encouraged more white flight, and poor economic conditions for the black population led to some violence during the 1960s.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Riots broke out in Wilmington in 1967 and again in 1968 in response to the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr, after which the National Guard occupied the city for nine months to prevent further violence.[55]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware is home to several festivals, fairs, and events.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Some of the more notable festivals are the Riverfest held in Seaford, the World Championship Punkin Chunkin formerly held at various locations throughout the state since 1986, the Rehoboth Beach Chocolate Festival, the Bethany Beach Jazz Funeral to mark the end of summer, the Apple Scrapple Festival held in Bridgeville, the Clifford Brown Jazz Festival in Wilmington, the Rehoboth Beach Jazz Festival, the Sea Witch Halloween Festival and Parade in Rehoboth Beach, the Rehoboth Beach Independent Film Festival, the Nanticoke Indian Pow Wow in Oak Orchard, Firefly Music Festival, and the Return Day Parade held after every election in Georgetown.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Delaware General Corporation Law (sometimes abbreviated DGCL), officially the General Corporation Law of the State of Delaware (Title 8, Chapter 1 of the Delaware Code), is the statute of the Delaware Code that governs corporate law in the U.S. state of Delaware.[2] The statute was adopted on March 10, 1899.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Since the 1913 anti-corporation reforms in New Jersey under the governorship of Woodrow Wilson, Delaware has become the most prevalent jurisdiction in United States corporate law and has been described as the de facto corporate capital of the United States.[3]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware charges no income tax on corporations not operating within the state, so taking advantage of Delaware's other benefits does not result in taxation.[18] At the same time, Delaware has a particularly aggressive tax on banks that locate in the state.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, in general, the state is viewed as a positive location for corporate tax purposes because favorable laws of incorporation allow companies to minimize corporate expenditures (achieved through legal standardization of corporate legal processes), creating a nucleus in Delaware with operating companies often in other states.[19]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In addition, Delaware has used its position as the state of incorporation to generate revenue from its abandoned and unclaimed property laws.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Under U.S. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Supreme Court precedent, the state of incorporation gets to keep any abandoned and unclaimed property, such as uncashed checks and unredeemed gift certificates, if the corporation does not have information about the location of the owner of the property.[20]  Abandoned property provides Delaware with about half a billion dollars annually.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Delaware House of Representatives has the lowest educational level of United States state legislatures.[8]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Thus,[neutrality is disputed] changes to the law are usually decided by the lawyers at the Corporation Law Council of the Delaware Bar and approved by the representatives.[9]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware has also attracted major credit card banks because of its relaxed rules regarding interest.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Many U.S. states have usury laws limiting the amount of interest a lender can charge. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Federal law allows a national bank to "import" these laws from the state in which its principal office is located.[12][page needed] Delaware (among others) has relatively relaxed interest laws,[13] so several national banks have decided to locate their principal office in Delaware.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>National banks are, however, corporations formed under federal law, not Delaware law.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>A corporation formed under Delaware state law benefits from the relaxed interest rules to the extent it conducts business in Delaware,[14] but is subject to restrictions of other states' laws if it conducts business in other states.[13]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>While most states require a for-profit corporation to have at least one director and two officers, Delaware laws do not have this restriction.[16] All offices may be held by a single person who also can be the sole shareholder.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The person, who does not need to be a U.S. citizen or resident, may also operate anonymously with only the listing agent through whom the company is registered named.[17]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In February 2013, The Economist published an article on tax-friendly jurisdictions, commenting that Delaware stood for "Dollars and Euros Laundered And Washed At Reasonable Expense".<</Q_RELEVANT>> Jeffrey W. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Bullock, Delaware's Secretary of State, insists that the state has struck the right balance between curbing criminality and "paying deference to the millions of legitimate businesspeople who benefit" from hassle-free incorporation.[22]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware Department of State, Division of Corporations – official website, corporation name search.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Delaware is considered a corporate haven because of its business-friendly corporate laws compared to most other U.S. states.[4][3] 66% of the Fortune 500, including Walmart and Amazon (two of the world's largest companies by revenue) are incorporated (and therefore have their domiciles for service of process purposes) in the state.[5] Over half of all publicly traded corporations listed in the New York Stock Exchange (including its owner, Intercontinental Exchange) are incorporated in Delaware.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>On June 30, 2013, Delaware Governor Jack Markell signed amendments[clarification needed] to the Delaware General Corporation Law.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The new legislation took effect on August 1, 2013, except for the ratification of the defective corporate acts amendment which took effect in 2014.[26]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The statute has been credited with reducing the tax burdens on Delaware residents as revenues from the statute provide two-fifths of the state's budget.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It has also been criticized for facilitating tax dodging and money laundering by multinational corporations, and for providing safe haven to money launderers, kleptocratic foreign rulers, and human traffickers.[3]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The trip was the first orbital spaceflight with only private citizens aboard and was part of a charitable effort on behalf of St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis, Tennessee.[3]  Isaacman was named mission commander.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The hospital selected two commercial astronauts: cancer survivor Hayley Arceneaux and military veteran Christopher Sembroski.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Shift4 selected entrepreneur Sian Proctor, who was named pilot.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Inspiration4 was led by Shift4 Payments CEO Jared Isaacman, an experienced pilot with qualification in military jets.[11][12] Isaacman procured the flight and its four seats from SpaceX and donated two of the seats to St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Jude. Hayley Arceneaux, a physician assistant at the hospital and a survivor of bone cancer, was selected by the hospital to board the flight.[13] St. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Jude raffled the second seat as part of a successful campaign to raise US$200 million for the hospital, termed St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Jude Mission: Inspired.[14][15] A raffle draw competition was held, in which entrants needed to be a US citizen and had to donate a significant amount of money between US$10 to US$10,000.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Kyle Hippchen, from Embry–Riddle Aeronautical University, donated US$600 and ultimately won the raffle but decided to give the seat to his friend, U.S.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Air Force veteran Christopher Sembroski, who had also entered the raffle by donating US$50. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Hippchen weighed in over the allowed limit.[16][17][18][19] Entrepreneur Sian Proctor was selected by Shift4 Payments to board the flight through a competition modeled after Shark Tank that rewarded the best business idea to make use of Shift4's commerce solutions.[20] The panelists in the competition included Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, Fast Company editor Stephanie Mehta, former NASA engineer Mark Rober and Bar Rescue host Jon Taffer.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Media coverage of the mission has been widely positive, noting its charitable focus, duration and altitude achieved.[42][43] The mission was documented in real time in a five-episode docuseries entitled Countdown: Inspiration4 Mission to Space, released on the subscription streaming service Netflix in September 2021.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The crew also starred in a Netflix special named "A StoryBots Space Adventure" released also in Netflix.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The special is also posted in Youtube.[44]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Inspiration4 (stylized as Inspirati④n) was a 2021 human spaceflight operated by SpaceX on behalf of Shift4 Payments CEO Jared Isaacman.[3] The mission launched the Crew Dragon Resilience on September 16, 2021, at 00:02:56 UTC[a] from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39A atop a Falcon 9 launch vehicle.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It placed the Dragon capsule into a low Earth orbit.[4] The mission ended on September 18, 2021, at 23:06:49 UTC,[4] when Resilience splashed down in the Atlantic Ocean.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Inspiration4 was the first human spaceflight to orbit Earth with only private citizens on board.[5][b] The trip promoted and raised money for St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Jude Children's Research Hospital. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The crew and trip intended to raise upwards of US$100 million to expand St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Jude's childhood cancer research.[7][8][9] Isaacman and his wife, Monica, personally donated US$125 million to the hospital, and contributions by SpaceX founder Elon Musk (US$55 million) and many others ultimately raised the total given to St.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Jude to more than US$243 million, far more than initial target amount.[10]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Inspiration4 mission was the second flight of Resilience, following its use for Crew-1.[20][24] It also marked the fourth crewed flight of a Crew Dragon.[25] The spacecraft's docking adapter, normally used to dock with the International Space Station, was replaced for this mission by a single monolithic multi-layer domed plexiglass[26] window inspired by the Cupola module, allowing 360° views outside Resilience's nose.[27] The cupola was protected during launch and re-entry by the spacecraft's retractable nosecone, which also housed a custom camera, enabling photography of the vehicle's interior and exterior during flight.[28] The cupola is removable so that Resilience can easily be reconfigured for missions in the future that require docking.[28] Four Draco thrusters on the spacecraft's nose necessitated the installation of four heat shield tiles on the cupola's exterior, which protected the plexiglass dome from engine exhaust during propulsive maneuvers.[28]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

As the second-stage engine of SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket cut off, Arceneaux reached into a pouch strapped to her leg and pulled out a plush toy dog that represents the therapy dogs employed by St. Jude. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The toy, attached to a tether, began to float above Arceneaux's head and in doing so fulfilled its purpose as the Inspiration4 mission's "zero-g indicator".<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Hanging in the air, it provided a visual signal to Arceneaux and her three crewmates that they were now in the microgravity environment of outer space after reaching Earth orbit on September 16, 2021.[34]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The river rises in the Poconos region of northeastern Pennsylvania in several ponds in Lehigh Township in Wayne County, approximately 15 miles (24 km) southeast of Scranton. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The PA Gazetteer of Streams shows that the Lehigh River begins as the outflow of Pocono Peak Lake.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Flowing south from the south end of the lake (a natural but dammed body of water), the river turns west after a mile and receives water from many lakes and ponds as it flows past Gouldsboro.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>It flows initially southwest, forming part of the border between Lackawanna County, Wayne County and Monroe County, passing through Francis E.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Walter Dam. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Near White Haven, it turns south, following a zigzag whitewater course through Lehigh Gorge State Park to Jim Thorpe, then southeast, past Lehighton.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Southeast of Lehighton, it passes through Blue Mountain in the narrow opening at Lehigh Gap. <<Q_RELEVANT>>A six-mile stretch of the river between Freemansburg and Easton is known as the "dry-lands" because all of the water from rain drainage flows underground.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Over the years since 2005 various groups such as the Lehigh Coldwater Fishery Alliance and the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission have worked with the Army Corps of Engineers to design annual flow plans[3] from the Frances Walter Dam (F.E.W.) to maximize the cold water discharge through the spring and summer.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This has helped enhance the population of coldwater species like brown trout to gain a growing naturally reproducing population within the river below F.E.W. dam all the way to Northampton.[4]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Part of the Lehigh River and a number of its tributaries are designated Pennsylvania Scenic Rivers by the state's Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The river's name is an anglicisation of the Lenape name for the river, Lechewuekink, which means "where there are forks".<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Both Lehigh County and Lehigh Valley are named for the river.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>According to an environmental report from a Pennsylvania nonprofit research center, the Lehigh River watershed is ranked second nationally in the volume of toxic substances released into it in 2020.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The study mirrored a previous report by the state's Department of Environmental Protection that found most of the county's waterways unsafe for swimming or aquatic life.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Between 1821 and 1966, the Lehigh River was owned by the Lehigh Coal and Navigation Company, making it the only privately owned river in the United States.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This private ownership continued until a local representative, Samuel Frank, promoted a bill to return control of the river to the state in 1967.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Lehigh River flows in a highly winding course through valleys between ridges of Pennsylvania's Appalachian Mountains.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Its upper course is characterized by numerous whitewater rapids and supports recreational pursuits, including rafting, kayaking, and canoeing.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Its lower course forms the heart of the Lehigh Valley, a historically important anthracite coal and steel-producing region of Pennsylvania.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Lehigh River is a whitewater river with Class I, II, and III rapids.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The most popular section of the Lehigh River for whitewater rafting, kayaking, and canoeing is through the Lehigh Gorge State Park.[5] The Lehigh Gorge State Park begins at the Francis E.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Walter Dam and ends in Jim Thorpe. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Several white water outfitters operate guided white water rafting trips in various sections of the river.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The first rafting outfitter on the Lehigh River was Whitewater Challengers, which was founded in 1975[failed verification].<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Water releases from the Francis E.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Walter Dam provide enough water to make the river deep enough for boating.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Three popular boating trips on the Lehigh River are:[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

St. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Luke's University Health Network<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Lehigh River (/ˈliːhaɪ/) is a 109-mile-long (175 km)[1] tributary of the Delaware River in eastern Pennsylvania.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The river flows in a generally southward pattern from the Pocono Mountains in Northeastern Pennsylvania through Allentown and much of the Lehigh Valley before joining the Delaware River in Easton.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>From the Lehigh Gap, the river flows southeast to Allentown, where it is joined by Little Lehigh Creek, then northeast past Bethlehem, where it joins the Delaware River in Easton at Pennsylvania's border with northwestern New Jersey.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Lehigh River holds many species of fish, including trout, smallmouth bass, largemouth bass, pickerel, panfish, carp, catfish, eel, and muskie.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Rainbow trout, brown trout, and brook trout in the 11"-14" range are average, while some have been caught in the 20" range. Smallmouth bass are large in numbers but are of smaller size with most between 8"-14" with an occasional fish from the 18"-21" range. There is an increasing number of muskie being reported within the 30"-52" range. There are both pure and tiger muskie, the usually sterile, hybrid offspring of the true muskellunge (Esox masquinongy) and the northern pike (Esox lucius) being caught in the river.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Roman numeral M represents the number 1000, though it was not used in Roman times.<</Q_RELEVANT>> There is, however, scant evidence that the letter was later introduced in the early centuries A.D. by the Romans.[3]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In English, ⟨m⟩ represents the voiced bilabial nasal /m/.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Oxford English Dictionary (first edition) says that ⟨m⟩ is sometimes a vowel, such as in words like spasm and in the suffix -ism.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In modern terminology, this is described as a syllabic consonant (IPA: /m̩/).

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The letter ⟨m⟩ represents the voiced bilabial nasal /m/ in the orthography of Latin as well as in those of many modern languages.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In Spanish, final ⟨m⟩ is rare and mostly corresponds to /n/, with /m/ being a foreign pronunciation applied only by some speakers in loanwords.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In Washo, lower-case ⟨m⟩ represents a voiced bilabial nasal /m/, while upper-case ⟨M⟩ represents a voiceless bilabial nasal /m̥/.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In the International Phonetic Alphabet, ⟨m⟩ represents the voiced bilabial nasal /m/.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Unit prefix M (mega), meaning one million times, and m (milli) meaning one-thousandth.[4][5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>m is the standard abbreviation for metre (or meter) in the International System of Units (SI).[4] However, m is sometimes also used as an abbreviation for mile.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>M often represents male or masculine, especially in conjunction with F for female or feminine.[4][5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In English, ⟨m⟩ represents the voiced bilabial nasal /m/.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Oxford English Dictionary (first edition) says that ⟨m⟩ is sometimes a vowel, such as in words like spasm and in the suffix -ism.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In modern terminology, this is described as a syllabic consonant (IPA: /m̩/).

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The letter ⟨m⟩ represents the voiced bilabial nasal /m/ in the orthography of Latin as well as in those of many modern languages.<</Q_RELEVANT>> In Spanish, final ⟨m⟩ is rare and mostly corresponds to /n/, with /m/ being a foreign pronunciation applied only by some speakers in loanwords.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In Washo, lower-case ⟨m⟩ represents a voiced bilabial nasal /m/, while upper-case ⟨M⟩ represents a voiceless bilabial nasal /m̥/.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In the International Phonetic Alphabet, ⟨m⟩ represents the voiced bilabial nasal /m/.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Unit prefix M (mega), meaning one million times, and m (milli) meaning one-thousandth.[4][5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>m is the standard abbreviation for metre (or meter) in the International System of Units (SI).[4] However, m is sometimes also used as an abbreviation for mile.[5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>M often represents male or masculine, especially in conjunction with F for female or feminine.[4][5]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Eastern Time Zone (ET)[1] is a time zone encompassing part or all of 23 states in the eastern United States, parts of eastern Canada, some Caribbean islands and the state of Quintana Roo in Mexico.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Most areas in the time zone observe daylight saving time and thus alternate between:<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The boundaries of the Eastern Time Zone have moved westward since the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) took over time-zone management from railroads in 1938.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The easternmost and northernmost counties in Kentucky were added to the zone in the 1940s, and in 1961, most of the state went Eastern.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2000, Wayne County, on the Tennessee border, switched from Central to Eastern Time.[5] Within the United States, the Eastern Time Zone is the most populous region, with nearly half of the country's population.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Washington, D.C., and 17 states are located entirely within the Eastern Time Zone.<</Q_RELEVANT>> They are:

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Five states are divided between the Eastern Time Zone and the Central Time Zone.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The following locations observe Eastern Time:<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The boundary between time zones is set forth in Title 49 of the Code of Federal Regulations with the boundary between the Eastern and Central Time Zones being specifically detailed in Part 71.[12]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Quintana Roo is the only Mexican state to observe Eastern Standard Time (Zona Sureste; Southeast Zone), after successful lobbying effort by tourism interests to move from Central Time.[16] Quintana Roo does not observe daylight saving time.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>For those in the United States, daylight saving time for the Eastern Time Zone was introduced by the Uniform Time Act of 1966, which specified that it would run from the last Sunday of April until the last Sunday in October.[9] The act was amended to make the first Sunday in April the beginning of daylight saving time beginning in 1987.[9] Later, the Energy Policy Act of 2005 extended daylight saving time in the United States, beginning in 2007.[9]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Within Canada, as with the United States, the Eastern Time Zone is the most populous time zone.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Most of Canada observes daylight saving time synchronously with the United States, with the exception of Saskatchewan, Yukon,[11] and several other very localized areas.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Southampton Island in Nunavut observes Eastern Standard Time year-round.[10]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Areas in the Eastern Time Zone which do not observe daylight saving time use Eastern Standard Time,[2] which is based on the 75th meridian west of Greenwich.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Observation of daylight saving time starts on the second Sunday in March; at 2:00 a.m.<</Q_RELEVANT>> EST, clocks are advanced to 3:00 a.m. EDT, creating a 23-hour day. On the first Sunday in November, at 2:00 a.m. EDT, clocks are moved back to 1:00 a.m. EST, which results in a 25-hour day.[3][4]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Turks and Caicos Islands followed Eastern Time with daylight saving until 2015, when the territory switched to the Atlantic Time Zone.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Turks and Caicos Islands switched back to the pre-2015 schedule in March 2018.[17] A 2017 consultation paper highlighted the advantage for business and tourism of being in the same time zone as the eastern United States as an important factor in the decision.[18]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Official U.S. time, including for the Eastern Time Zone<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The time in this zone is based on the mean solar time of the 75th meridian west of the Royal Observatory, Greenwich.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>U.S. time zone map; Archived February 15, 2009, at the Wayback Machine<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>History of U.S. time zones and UTC conversion; Archived August 8, 2011, at the Wayback Machine<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In March 2019, the Florida Legislature passed a bill requesting authorization from Congress for year-round daylight saving time, which would effectively put Florida on Eastern Daylight Time year-round (except for west of the Apalachicola River, which would be on Central Daylight Time year-round).[6] A similar bill was proposed for the Canadian province of Ontario by its legislative assembly in late 2020,[7] which passed though was placed on hold until Quebec and New York agreed to make the same change, which had not happened as of 2024.[8]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Additionally, Phenix City, Alabama, and several nearby communities in Russell County, Alabama, unofficially observe Eastern Time.[14] This is due to their close proximity to Columbus, Georgia, which is on Eastern Time.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In addition Smiths Station in Lee County along with Valley and Lanett in Chambers County observe Eastern Time.[15]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Bahamas and Haiti officially observe Eastern Time with daylight saving time.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Cuba generally follows the U.S. with Eastern Standard Time in the winter, and Eastern Daylight Time in the summer, but the exact day of change varies year to year.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The Cayman Islands, Jamaica, and Navassa Island use Eastern Standard Time year-round.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), which is four hours behind Coordinated Universal Time (UTC−04:00) and observed during spring/summer/early autumn.<</Q_RELEVANT>>
